title: The body: its parts
hook: like a bag of mixed grain opened and looked at: hair, nails, teeth, skin (MN 10)

segments.voice: Yesterday's word was sampajanna, clear knowing, and your line was even this: no part of the day left out. Day two hundred fifty-three.

Think how much of a day goes into what the body looks like. The mirror in the morning. The photo retaken four times. The comparison that slips in while scrolling. The body becomes one picture, judged good or bad. The Satipatthana Sutta does something different. It opens the body up, piece by piece, with the calm of a farmer checking stored grain.
screen: `THE MIRROR, THE RETAKEN PHOTO.` → `ONE PICTURE, JUDGED.` → `PIECE BY PIECE.`

segments.voice: The practitioner reviews this very body, the sutta says, from the soles of the feet up and from the top of the head down, bounded by skin and, in the sutta's blunt word, full of many kinds of impurity. Then the list: hair of the head, hair of the body, nails, teeth, skin, flesh, sinews, bones, marrow, and on inward, organs and fluids, thirty-one parts in the sutta's list. Later tradition added the brain to make thirty-two. Then the image. A bag with an opening at both ends, full of mixed grain: hill rice, red rice, beans, peas, sesame, husked rice. A person with good eyes opens it and looks: this is rice, these are beans, this is sesame. Notice the tone. They aren't disgusted, and they aren't admiring. They're just sorting, clearly. That's the heart of the practice. In the Buddhist tradition, this contemplation is used to loosen two strong pulls: vanity about the body and craving for other bodies. Some teachers stress the unattractiveness of the parts; others, especially today, stress simple, neutral seeing. Either way, the point is not to hate the body. It's to see it as it is: not a single image to be judged, but a working collection of many things, each doing its job. Hair is hair. Teeth are teeth. The picture in the mirror loosens its grip a little.
screen: `FROM THE SOLES UP, THE HEAD DOWN.` · `HAIR, NAILS, TEETH, SKIN.` · `A BAG OF MIXED GRAIN, OPENED.` · `SORTING, NOT JUDGING.` · then, large: `A BAG OF GRAIN.`

segments.voice: Name ten parts of your body slowly, feeling each one if you can: hair, nails, teeth, skin, bones, muscles, heart, lungs, blood, breath. No admiring or wincing, just the calm of someone sorting grain: this is that. If any part is painful or hard to think about today, skip it gently and move on.
The body, its parts. Opened like a bag of mixed grain and sorted calmly: hair, nails, teeth, skin, each one just what it is.
Your line: a bag of grain. Sorted, not judged: each part just what it is. Day two hundred fifty-three.

howItsDone: In Theravada monasteries, the first five parts (hair of the head, body hair, nails, teeth, skin) are traditionally taught to new monks and nuns at ordination; the contemplation of the thirty-two parts is recited and practiced to loosen vanity and craving.

chat.says: Isn't thinking of your body as hair, bones and organs a way of hating it?
options: No, it's calm sorting, like checking a bag of grain: not disgusted, not admiring.
Yes, it's meant to make you ashamed of having a body at all.
No, it's a way to admire how beautifully each part of you is made.
chat.meaning: Like someone sorting grain, the practitioner just sees: this is rice, these are beans. The point is seeing the body as it is, not hating it.

notes: Sensitivity: this contemplation (asubha / paṭikūlamanasikāra) can be hard for people with eating disorders or body image struggles; the script frames it as neutral sorting and invites skipping any part. Please confirm the framing is faithful and acceptable.
Thirty-one parts in MN 10, thirty-two with the brain in the Khuddakapāṭha: confirm.
The grains in the simile (hill paddy, paddy, green gram, cow-peas, sesame, husked rice) vary by translation; the script simplifies them. Please check.
Ordination teaching of the first five parts (tacapañcaka): confirm.
